question: The metal which will NOT displace lead from its salt solution is:
solution:
The correct answer is __**Copper**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The ability of one metal to displace another from its salt solution depends on the **Reactivity Series** of metals. This series ranks metals based on their chemical reactivity, primarily their ability to lose electrons and form **positive ions**.
 
• A **displacement reaction** is a type of chemical reaction where a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound. In the context of metals, a metal higher in the reactivity series will displace any metal placed below it from its aqueous salt solution.
 
• **Aluminium** is significantly more reactive than **Lead**. In the reactivity series, **Aluminium (Al)** is positioned much higher than **Lead (Pb)**. Therefore, if Aluminium is added to a lead salt solution, it will displace the lead. ***Hence, the statement regarding Aluminium is incorrect for this question.***
 
• **Calcium** and **Magnesium** are highly reactive metals belonging to the **Alkaline Earth Metals** group. Both **Calcium (Ca)** and **Magnesium (Mg)** sit high up in the reactivity series, well above **Lead (Pb)**. They can easily displace Lead from its salt solution. ***Hence, the statements regarding Calcium and Magnesium are incorrect for this question.***
 
• **Copper (Cu)** is placed below **Lead (Pb)** in the reactivity series. Since Copper is less reactive than Lead, it does not possess the chemical potential to displace Lead ions from a solution. ***Hence, the statement regarding Copper is correct as it will NOT displace lead.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The Reactivity Series:**

 
 
• The series follows a general order: **Potassium (K)** > **Sodium (Na)** > **Calcium (Ca)** > **Magnesium (Mg)** > **Aluminium (Al)** > **Zinc (Zn)** > **Iron (Fe)** > **Tin (Sn)** > **Lead (Pb)** > **Hydrogen (H)** > **Copper (Cu)** > **Mercury (Hg)** > **Silver (Ag)** > **Gold (Au)**.
 
• Metals like **Potassium** and **Sodium** are so reactive they are often stored in **kerosene** to prevent reaction with moisture in the air.
 
• Metals at the bottom, such as **Gold** and **Platinum**, are known as **noble metals** because they are extremely unreactive and do not easily corrode or react with acids.
 
 
 
• **Displacement Reaction Mechanism:**
 
 
• In these reactions, the more reactive metal undergoes **oxidation** (loses electrons), while the less reactive metal ion in the solution undergoes **reduction** (gains electrons).
 
• For example, if **Magnesium** is put into **Lead Nitrate** solution, the Magnesium atoms turn into ions, and Lead ions turn into solid metallic Lead.
 
• Since **Copper** is lower than **Lead**, it cannot force its electrons onto Lead ions; therefore, no reaction occurs when Copper is placed in a Lead salt solution.
 
 
 
• **Lead (Pb):**
 
 
• **Lead** has the atomic number **82**. It is a heavy metal that is denser than most common materials.
 
• It is relatively resistant to corrosion but is placed above **Hydrogen** in the reactivity series, meaning it can theoretically displace hydrogen from dilute acids, though the reaction is often slowed by the formation of insoluble coatings.
 
 
 
• **Copper (Cu):**
 
 
• **Copper** has the atomic number **29**. It is a transition metal known for high **thermal and electrical conductivity**.
 
• It is one of the few metals that occur in nature in a directly usable metallic form (native metals). Because it is below **Hydrogen** and **Lead**, it is considered a relatively stable and unreactive metal in many environments.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Electrochemical Context:** The reactivity series is fundamentally linked to **Standard Reduction Potentials**. Metals with a more negative reduction potential are more reactive and act as stronger **reducing agents**.
 
• **Practical Application:** This principle is used in **Galvanization**, where **Zinc** (more reactive) is used to coat **Iron** to prevent rusting. The Zinc displaces the corrosive action from the Iron by acting as a sacrificial anode.
 
• **Metal Extraction:** The reactivity of a metal determines the method used to extract it from its ore. Highly reactive metals like **Aluminium** are extracted via **electrolysis**, while less reactive metals like **Lead** or **Iron** can be extracted by reduction with **Carbon**.
